scaling.name: Scaling
scaling.intro: AI progress has been driven above all by scale: training with more compute, power and data has reliably produced better models. We track how fast those inputs are growing and whether that growth can continue through the end of the decade.
focus: Training compute trends for frontier models
Hardware and power constraints on future training runs

software-progress.name: Software progress
software-progress.intro: Better algorithms, cleaner data and new training techniques let models reach the same capability with less compute. We measure how quickly these efficiency gains, often called algorithmic progress, are arriving and what drives them.
focus: What software progress means for future capabilities

open-models.name: Open models
open-models.intro: Some of the most capable AI systems can be downloaded and run by anyone, while others stay proprietary. We track how far open-weight models trail the closed frontier and how quickly that gap is closing.
focus: The lag between open and closed models
How fast frontier capabilities become widely available
Open models on capability and cyber benchmarks

capabilities.name: Capabilities
capabilities.intro: AI systems now write code, pass professional exams and assist with research, and they improve quickly. Measuring exactly what they can and cannot do is hard, so we track capabilities across many tasks and benchmarks.
focus: The Epoch Capabilities Index across models
Where benchmark scores and real-world performance diverge

math.name: Math
math.intro: Mathematics is one of the clearest tests of AI reasoning: answers can be checked automatically and the hardest problems reach the edge of human knowledge. FrontierMath, our own benchmark, measures how far today’s best systems can go.
focus: FrontierMath Tiers 1–4, Open Problems and Erdős
AI use acknowledged in math research
How math ability changes with each model generation

leading-companies.name: Leading companies
leading-companies.intro: A handful of companies build the world’s most powerful AI systems, and the landscape changes fast. We track the leading labs, their model releases, compute resources and workforce.
focus: Revenue, funding and staff of frontier labs

finances.name: Finances
finances.intro: AI attracts unprecedented investment in hardware, data centers and talent, and costs are rising fast. We track what it costs to train and run models, how much companies spend and earn, and how hardware prices move.

geopolitics.name: Geopolitics
geopolitics.intro: AI development is concentrated in a few countries, with the United States and China far ahead. Export controls, infrastructure and trade shape who can build the most advanced systems, and we track how compute and capability are distributed globally.
focus: Where AI compute ends up, by country

chips.name: Chips
chips.intro: Specialized AI chips sit at the center of a global competition for compute. We track their performance, energy efficiency and price-performance, along with the supply chains that decide who gets the most advanced hardware.
focus: Quarterly AI chip sales by designer
Supply chain components such as HBM and packaging

data-centers.name: Data centers
data-centers.intro: Frontier AI runs in vast facilities packed with chips that draw as much power as small cities, some built in under two years. Using satellite imagery and permits, we track their scale, cost, compute and power.
focus: Compute capacity and power per site
Who owns and uses the largest sites

energy.name: Energy
energy.intro: The power needed to train frontier models has been roughly doubling each year, and new data centers put real pressure on grids. Hardware efficiency improves too, but compute demand has been growing faster.

adoption-and-use.name: Adoption and use
adoption-and-use.intro: AI tools reach hundreds of millions of people, yet reliable data on who uses them, and how, is scarce. Through original polling and research we study how AI is adopted and what drives or limits uptake.
focus: How Americans use AI at home and at work
AI use acknowledged in scientific papers

economic-impact.name: Economic impact
economic-impact.intro: AI may reshape the economy more than any technology in generations, but the size and timing of the effects remain uncertain. We combine empirical research with formal economic models of automation, jobs, wages and growth.
focus: Whether AI could accelerate economic growth

future-of-ai.name: Future of AI
future-of-ai.intro: How powerful will AI become, and how fast? We build quantitative forecasts, from near-term compute and capability trends to longer-term questions about when AI might become transformative.
focus: What current trends imply for the next decade

ai-impacts.name: AI impacts observatory
ai-impacts.intro: A dashboard of nine real-world indicators across five domains that AI might be changing, from cyber incidents to how people work. Each indicator is tracked over time so changes show up early.
focus: AI at work and at home

chatgpt-usage.text: Aggregate metadata from the recorded ChatGPT histories of 5,000 US YouGov panelists, December 2022 to December 2025.

cyber-vulnerabilities.title: Cyber vulnerabilities
cyber-vulnerabilities.text: Trends in software and hardware vulnerabilities (CVEs) since 2020: how counts and severity have changed, broken down by the organizations that report them.

frontier-lab-hiring.title: Frontier lab hiring
frontier-lab-hiring.text: A daily archive of job postings at Anthropic and OpenAI.

eci.title: Epoch Capabilities Index
eci.text: The ECI combines scores from many AI benchmarks into a single general-capability scale, so models can be compared even across timespans long enough for individual benchmarks to saturate.
facts: ECI points gained per year at the frontier

sections.p: Single benchmarks saturate quickly. Pooling many of them on one scale keeps comparisons meaningful as models improve.
Since November 2026 the ECI uses a Bayesian model, which gives better-justified uncertainty estimates and lets models be compared directly.
Alongside the general index there are presets for software engineering, math and cyber capabilities.

frontiermath.title: FrontierMath
frontiermath.text: Our program for testing AI on advanced mathematics, from unpublished competition-style problems to open research questions mathematicians have not solved.

sections.p: Several hundred unpublished, highly challenging problems. Tiers 1–3 run from undergraduate to advanced graduate level; Tier 4 is research-level mathematics.
Significant unsolved problems; an AI solution would meaningfully advance human mathematical knowledge.
A curated set of Erdős problems where models must write solutions in Lean. GPT-6.1 Sol leads so far with 3 of 68 solved.

frontiermath-open-problems.title: FrontierMath: Open Problems
frontiermath-open-problems.text: Unsolved mathematics problems that have resisted serious attempts by professional mathematicians. Recently expanded to 50 problems, with support from Schmidt Sciences.
facts: solved by humans and AI together

sections.p: Moderately interesting: 6 of 22. Solid result: 2 of 18. Major advance: 1 of 6. Breakthrough: 1 of 3.
Organizations can request access to the solution verifiers used to check proposed answers.

mirrorcode.title: MirrorCode
mirrorcode.text: A benchmark for long-horizon coding, co-developed with METR: models must reimplement an entire program end to end, without ever seeing its source code.
facts: output match required, including held-out tests

sections.p: Most coding benchmarks test short tasks such as fixing a bug or adding a feature. MirrorCode tests whether a model can rebuild a whole program.
Targets span Unix utilities, data serialization and query tools, bioinformatics, interpreters and more.

epoch-automation-reports.title: Epoch Automation Reports
epoch-automation-reports.text: Realistic, open-ended tasks drawn from Epoch AI’s own work. Models produce real work outputs, and human graders score them against the standard expected of an Epoch employee.

table.caption: Mean rubric score by task category (100% meets the internal standard)

sections.p: Scores on real internal tasks show how close agents are to automating day-to-day research work, not just answering test questions.
